passage: So in the debate about school plastic, I didn't just say "plastic is bad". I'm Keerthana, and I told the class to imagine their water bottles lined up from here to the gate, every single day. I drew a little diagram of a bottle's journey on the board. People sat up. Later, Sahil, you asked, "Where did you get the fact about the gate?" and I realised I'd picked the most dramatic example and hadn't checked the source properly. I went home, looked it up and corrected it next day. Good examples persuade, but they have to be true.

qa.q: What did Keerthana draw on the board?
qa.a: Keerthana drew a little diagram of a bottle's journey.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling when Sahil asked about the source?
qa.a: Keerthana was uneasy and realised the most dramatic example had been picked without checking. Keerthana then corrected it.

qa.q: What could Keerthana do the next time an example is used?
qa.a: Check the source before using it and pick examples that are fair, not just dramatic. Vivid examples help only if they're accurate.

qa.q: How might Sahil have seen Keerthana's debate?
qa.a: Sahil found it persuasive but asked about the source, which shows a care for accuracy. That question led Keerthana to fix it.

grounding: A teenager uses examples and a diagram to persuade peers, and learns to check sources so they are not cherry-picked.

passage: Zainab stood in front of the class to argue for earlier bedtimes. She didn't quote a rule. She said, "Your phone at ten per cent is like you at midnight, slow and grumpy." The class laughed. She drew a battery diagram on the board, and half of them nodded. I'm Rehana and I noticed she'd only picked examples that supported her. At the break I asked, "What about people who work better late?" Zainab thought, then said, "Fair. I should check that." She said she'd look for a source and add the other side in her next talk.

qa.q: What did Zainab draw on the board?
qa.a: She drew a battery diagram.

qa.q: What was Zainab feeling when Rehana asked about people who work better late?
qa.a: She was probably caught off guard but curious rather than defensive, since she paused, said 'Fair' and promised to check.

qa.q: What could Zainab do to make her argument stronger?
qa.a: Look for a source and include the other side too. Vivid examples help but can be cherry-picked.

qa.q: How does Rehana see Zainab's talk?
qa.a: Rehana finds it vivid and effective but notices the examples were one-sided, and asks kindly.

grounding: A teenager uses an analogy and diagram to persuade, and an observer notes examples can be cherry-picked, so checking matters.

passage:
Monday: In the debate on banning plastic bottles, Arnab held up a photo of a turtle tangled in plastic. "This is what happens!" The class gasped. His team won.
Tuesday: Tejas, on the losing side, came up to him. "Where's that photo from? And your number about ninety percent of fish having plastic, where's that from?"
Arnab didn't know. He'd found it on a random video.
Wednesday: Arnab searched the library and the environment ministry website. The turtle photo was real, from another coast. But the ninety percent was wrong; the real number he found was much smaller.
Friday: At the next debate, Arnab used the turtle photo again, but this time with the source, and corrected the number. Tejas nodded. "Now I believe you."

qa.q: What did Arnab hold up in the debate?
qa.a: A photo of a turtle tangled in plastic.

qa.q: What was Arnab feeling when Tejas asked for his sources?
qa.a: Arnab felt caught out and uneasy, realising he didn't know where his facts came from.

qa.q: What did Arnab do that improved his argument?
qa.a: He checked reliable sources, corrected the wrong number, and cited where his example came from.

qa.q: How did Tejas see Arnab's first argument?
qa.a: Tejas was skeptical of the vivid example and the number, suspecting they weren't properly sourced.

grounding: Over a week, a teenager uses a vivid example to persuade peers, then learns to check sources after being questioned.

passage:
"Aadhya, you're using that one story to win your debate? Let your Harsha Mama tell you something.
When I was in Class 11, I argued that mobile phones make students fail. My proof? One boy in my class who played games all night and failed. I told the story so well, everyone nodded.
Then the other team stood up and said, 'That's one boy. We asked forty students. Most who use phones for study did better.'
My face burned. I'd picked the one example that fit my point and ignored the rest.
So use examples, beta. They make your point come alive. But check whether they're the whole picture, or just the part you like."

qa.q: How many students did the other team ask?
qa.a: Forty students.

qa.q: What was young Harsha feeling when the other team responded?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed, his face burning, realising his example was cherry-picked.

qa.q: What choice inside the story could have made Harsha's argument stronger?
qa.a: Checking broader evidence instead of relying on one story would have made his argument fairer and stronger.

qa.q: How might the other team have felt answering Harsha's story?
qa.a: They probably felt confident, since their wider evidence showed his example wasn't the whole picture.

grounding: An uncle recalls using a cherry-picked example in a debate and learning to check the whole picture.

passage:
The science presentation was in fifteen minutes, and the projector had broken. Minakshi had planned to show a video of the heart pumping.
"Now what?" Harish panicked.
Minakshi grabbed a marker. "I'll draw it." She sketched a heart on the whiteboard, with arrows. "It's like a water pump in a village. It pushes blood to the body, then pulls it back."
Harish frowned. "Is that analogy right? Let me check." He flipped through the textbook. "It says the heart is a double pump. Two sides."
Minakshi added a second pump to her drawing. "Better. Left side to the body, right side to the lungs."
When they presented, the class understood straight away. The teacher said the analogy and diagram were clear and accurate.

qa.q: What did Minakshi compare the heart to?
qa.a: A water pump in a village.

qa.q: What was Harish feeling when the projector broke?
qa.a: Harish felt panicky and worried about the presentation.

qa.q: What did Harish do that improved the presentation?
qa.a: He checked the textbook to confirm the analogy, which made it more accurate.

qa.q: How might the class have experienced the diagram?
qa.a: The class understood it quickly, finding the drawing and analogy clear.

grounding: Under time pressure, a teenager uses an analogy and diagram to explain, and a partner checks the source for accuracy.

passage: Zeenat had one minute to convince the student council, squeezed into the Kochi school's AV room, to drop plastic cups from the annual fest. She held up a drawing: a single cup, an arrow to a drain, an arrow to the backwaters behind the school, then a fish. "Every cup we use on Friday ends up in our own canal," she said. "Remember the monsoon, when the drain by the canteen choked? I pulled cups out of it myself." Heads nodded. People remembered the smell. Then she added, "And a video says ninety percent of fish have plastic inside." Jomon, from class twelve, raised a hand. "Which video? Who measured?" Zeenat opened her mouth, then closed it. She didn't know. "I'll check that one," she said. "But the drain, you all saw." The vote passed. That night she hunted for the study and replaced the claim with one she could name.

qa.q: What did Zeenat's drawing show?
qa.a: It showed a single cup, a drain, the backwaters behind the school, and then a fish.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling when Jomon asked 'Which video?'
qa.a: Zeenat was probably caught off guard and a little embarrassed, since her mouth opened and closed and she didn't know the source. She may also have felt determined, because she promised to check instead of defending it.

qa.q: Which part of Zeenat's pitch was strongest, and what needed fixing?
qa.a: The drain story worked because everyone had seen it; the fish figure from an unnamed video needed checking, and replacing it with a named source fixed that.

qa.q: How might the council have reacted later if Jomon hadn't asked?
qa.a: They might have voted on a claim nobody could trace, and trusted Zeenat's examples less if it later turned out to be wrong.

grounding: It shows a teenager using a diagram and a shared memory to persuade peers, and learning to check the source behind a vivid claim.
